Chapter 45

What the compiler says: warnings, errors and the codes that name them

Every message Svelte prints has a code, and the code is the handle for everything you can do about it. Zero svelte-ignore comments, a check that fails on a warning, and the autofixer in verify; the warnings the code answers by its shape, the errors that explain why it is written the way it is, the runtime errors and warnings worth recognising on sight — and the one warning the build still prints, and why it stays.

By the end of this chapter

Read any Svelte diagnostic by its code, know the three places that code can be named, and fix the cause rather than the message.

Svelte talks to you in four voices. Compiler warnings — markup that will probably hurt somebody, like a clickable <div> — and compiler errors, code it refuses to compile. Then, once the code runs, runtime errors, which stop it, and runtime warnings, which the development build prints to the console. Each message carries a short snake_case code: state_referenced_locally, each_key_duplicate, await_waterfall. Svelte’s documentation lists every one under four pages with those names, and the codes are the handle for everything else in this chapter.

The bar this project keeps is simple to say. pnpm run check runs svelte-check with --fail-on-warnings (chapter 03), so a compiler warning fails verify and CI as surely as a type error does; and there is not one <!-- svelte-ignore --> comment anywhere in src — grep -rn svelte-ignore src finds nothing. Every warning the compiler could give was answered by changing the code, and the sections below show the answers. That is not because suppressing is wrong. It is because a suppression is a decision that outlives the reason for it, and a project with none has nothing to re-check when the reason goes away.

One code, three places to name it

A warning’s code is the same string in every tool that can act on it. In a component, <!-- svelte-ignore a11y_autofocus (because of reasons) --> above the line silences that one occurrence — the parenthesised reason is part of the syntax, and Svelte’s documentation shows it. For the whole project, svelte-check --compiler-warnings "css_unused_selector:error" turns a warning into an error or :ignore drops it; the flag’s own help text still spells codes the Svelte 4 way, with dashes, and Svelte 5’s have underscores — an old spelling in an ignore comment earns you legacy_code, and an unknown one unknown_code. And for the compiler itself, compilerOptions.warningFilter is a function that receives each Warning and returns true to keep it — vite-plugin-svelte’s onwarn is the bundler’s older hook for the same job. Three places, one string. This project uses none of them.

Warnings the code answers

options_missing_custom_element — “The customElement option is used when generating a custom element. Did you forget the customElement: true compile option?” — is what the embed component used to earn in every compile that was not the custom-element one: the server build, svelte-check, the autofixer. The component named its tag in <svelte:options customElement={{ tag }}>, which is what Svelte’s docs show, and the check script once silenced the warning for the whole project. The answer was to move the one thing the option did — define the tag — into this module, which only the two builds that compile the folder as a custom element ever load. The component became an ordinary component everywhere, the warning had nothing left to say, and the project-wide silence went (chapter 38).

state_referenced_locally — “This reference only captures the initial value of %name%. Did you mean to reference it inside a %type% instead?” — fires when a component reads a prop at the top of its script, because a prop can change and that read will not see it. Usually that is a bug, and the docs’ example is one: state passed into setContext by value, which the child then reads forever as its first value. Twice in this project it is the intent. The trip page is keyed on its slug, so a different trip is a different TripView, and its props are read once; the date picker takes its start and end as the *initial* value and owns the range after that. untrack(() => …) says “read this without subscribing”, which is exactly the claim, and the compiler takes it as an answer. A comment beside each says the same thing to a person.

css_unused_selector — “Unused CSS selector” — is the compiler noticing that a scoped rule matches nothing in the template, and removing it from the output. Here the rule matches attributes an attachment writes at run time, which the compiler cannot see. The docs give the answer in the warning’s own entry: “use :global to preserve the selector as-is” — and wrapping it in the parent element’s class keeps it from leaking beyond this page. This is the warning to treat with the most suspicion, because it is usually right: a selector the compiler cannot see matching is, nine times out of ten, a selector nothing matches.

The accessibility warnings are a third of the list, and each is a question about an element. The table is the project’s answers, element by element — the point being that every one is answered by markup a screen reader understands, never by an aria-* attribute that papers over the wrong element.

Errors the shape of the code answers

A module that wanted to share a theme would naturally write export let choice = $state('system'), and the compiler refuses: state_invalid_export — “Cannot export state from a module if it is reassigned. Either export a function returning the state value or only mutate the state value’s properties”. Its sibling derived_invalid_export says the same of $derived. The reason is mechanical: an importer receives the binding’s value at import time, and a rune’s reactivity lives in the variable, not the value, so a reassigned export would be a snapshot. The shape that answers it is a class with $state fields and one exported instance — theme.choice is a property read, which stays reactive. The module’s header says why one module-level instance is safe on a server here, against Svelte’s general advice to prefer context (chapter 23).

{const Icon = $derived(KIND_ICONS[k])} is a *declaration tag*, and it replaced {@const} in this project. The old tag had a placement rule — const_tag_invalid_placement: “{@const} must be the immediate child of {#snippet}, {#if}, {:else if}, {:else}, {#each} …” — and a value that was worked out once. A declaration tag is an ordinary const or let, its value is a rune like anywhere else ($derived here, so it follows k), and the only things it refuses are legacy mode (declaration_tag_no_legacy_mode) and anything that is not a let or const (declaration_tag_invalid_type). Chapter 49 counts the migration.

erasableSyntaxOnly is a TypeScript option answering a Svelte error before it can happen. Svelte strips the types from a lang="ts" block rather than compiling TypeScript, so a feature that *emits* JavaScript — an enum, a value namespace, a constructor parameter property — is typescript_invalid_feature: “TypeScript language features like %feature% are not natively supported … you will need to use a preprocessor”, with a pointer to vitePreprocess({ script: true }). That preprocessor would work, at the cost of running TypeScript over every component. Forbidding the features costs nothing — this codebase never wanted an enum — and Node’s type stripping for scripts/*.ts needs the same rule, so one option serves both.

Runtime warnings, in the console

The development build prints these; production does not. One of them is the one an async-first codebase meets first. await_waterfall — “An async derived, %name% was not read immediately after it resolved. This often indicates an unnecessary waterfall” — is two independent $derived(await …) in a row: the second is not even created until the first resolves. The documentation’s fix is to start both promises first, each in its own $derived, and await them after. The trip page has one await and the new-trip page one, which is the cheapest way to stay out of this warning’s way.

The autofixer as a gate

The compiler’s warnings are about what the code *does*; the Svelte autofixer’s suggestions are about how it is *written* — an $effect that assigns state another rune could derive, a bind:this an attachment would replace. pnpm run lint:svelte runs it over every component (chapter 03 builds the script) and fails on any suggestion that is neither followed nor answered in .autofixer-accepted.json, where each declined suggestion is recorded with the file, a piece of its text, how many times the file earns it, and a reason. The count is the teeth: a new occurrence of an accepted suggestion still fails, because it has not been read yet.

The one warning the build still prints

script_context_deprecated is real, and it is not this project’s code. mdsvex turns a guide’s front matter into a module script, and the latest stable release, 0.12.8, writes it as <script context="module"> — there is no option to change that, and its regular expression for “reuse an existing module script” only matches the old spelling, so a guide cannot pre-empt it with a <script module> of its own. The 1.0 line writes <script module>, and it is a prerelease. A warningFilter would make the build quiet, and it would also make it lie: the deprecation is true, and the day it becomes an error, the line will be the first thing to read. So it stays printed, and the upgrade is on the backlog in chapter 50. svelte-check never sees it, because it does not check .svx files — which is the one place --fail-on-warnings has a gap, and now you know where it is.

Checkpoint

  • You can name the four kinds of diagnostic and where Svelte documents each.
  • You know the three places a warning’s code can be named, and why this project uses none of them.
  • You can say how untrack, :global and a module-level customElements.define each answer a warning without silencing it.
  • You can explain state_invalid_export and the class-and-instance shape that answers it, and what erasableSyntaxOnly has to do with typescript_invalid_feature.
  • You can read effect_update_depth_exceeded and await_waterfall and say what to change.
